summary: Gregg Henriques, a professor who directs an APA-accredited program at James Madison University, explains what a 'psychological doctor' (PD) is by contrasting it with psychological researchers, psychiatrists, and allied mental health professionals. He defines a PD as a licensed professional psychologist trained in delivering health care services, lists ten core competencies from the JMU program, and illustrates the approach with a hypothetical case of an anxious college freshman named Tina, showing how a PD builds an assessment-based conceptualization and uses 'directive empathy.' The rest of the page is site navigation and unrelated article listings, which were ignored.
one_line: Gregg Henriques defines the 'psychological doctor' as a health service psychologist and contrasts the role with researchers, psychiatrists, and counselors using a college student case.
key_facts: Gregg Henriques directs an APA-accredited program that trains psychological doctors at the JMU Combined Clinical and School Program.
A psychological doctor is described as a health service provider who offers skills stemming from knowledge of the science of human psychology and training as an assessor and interventionist.
The Doctor of Psychology (PsyD) is described as the most direct marker of a psychological doctor, though many PhDs in clinical, counseling and school psychology are also psychological doctors.
Surveys of psychiatrists show that about 90% function primarily in a psychopharmacology role, according to the note.
Psychiatrists are described as medical doctors who are trained first in medicine before specializing in disorders of the psyche.
The JMU doc program lists ten fundamental competencies, the first being 'self-reflective awareness and interpersonal grace'.
The ten competencies include psychological assessment, psychological interventions, ethics and professional judgment, and research and scholarship.
The hypothetical case involves Tina, an 18-year-old college freshman from a small, rural town who is a first generation college student hoping to become a physician.
Tina's first semester grades were a 3.2, and she reported trouble sleeping, nightmares about failing out of school, and frequent stomach aches.
A psychiatrist would likely diagnose Tina according to the DSM-V based on a 20-minute interview and offer anti-anxiety or anti-depressant medication.
A professional counselor would typically meet Tina for 50 minutes a week in a warm, empathic, growth-oriented relationship.

A psychological doctor would begin with a 'psychological check-up' of empirically validated measures covering well-being, emotions, self-concept, relational style, personality, habits, and psychopathology screens.
The note defines 'directive empathy' as the process by which the practitioner guides the patient to understand and organize their experience via a working conceptual model of human psychology.
The author says a psychological doctor does not use medication and would typically see a client once a week.
Psychological researchers are described as research scientists who study mental processes and behaviors, with the largest portion working in university settings.
